questions.stem: A Riverbend customer raises three items in one chat: a $310 credit for four days without power in the March outage, an estimated electricity read she says is 40% too high, and a six-month plan for her $420 water bill. The agent may correct reads and set up plans itself. When the `PreToolUse` hook on `apply_bill_credit` denies a credit above $250, the agent now hands the whole chat to the human queue, and approvers, though short of time, spend about 10 minutes rebuilding each case. Which two changes should the agent make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Keep handing the whole chat to the human queue, but add a handoff that lists the three items with their evidence, so one approver settles them together.
options.explanation: The handoff is better, but two items the agent can settle itself still go to a person, so the approver keeps doing agent work and the contact doesn't count toward the 75% target. Handing over the whole chat would suit a customer who asks for a person.

options.text: Correct the estimated electricity read and set up the six-month water plan in this chat, because both are within the agent's own authority.
options.explanation: Splitting the request into items shows that the read correction and the water plan need no approval. Settling both now resolves two of the three items in the chat and leaves the approver only the decision that is really theirs.

options.text: Apply $250 of the outage credit now, the largest credit the agent may grant alone, and escalate the remaining $60 with the outage evidence.
options.explanation: It keeps each call under the limit, but a $310 credit is one decision that needs approval; splitting it routes around the rule instead of following it, and the approver sees a $60 request. Granting up to the limit would suit a request of $250 or less.

options.text: Escalate the $310 credit alone through `escalate_to_agent`, with the account ID, outage dates and hours, recommended amount, and what the agent has already done.
options.explanation: Only the $310 credit is above the $250 limit, so only it needs a person. A structured handoff with the account, the outage evidence, the recommended amount and what is already done lets the approver decide without spending 10 minutes rebuilding the case.

options.text: Settle the three items in this chat, applying the $310 credit because the outage record in `get_account` confirms the four days without power.
options.explanation: Strong evidence doesn't change who may approve: credits above $250 need a human approver, and the hook denies the call anyway. The agent should settle what it can and pass the credit decision to a person.

questions.keyConcept: Split a multi-concern request into items, resolve those within authority, and escalate only the item that needs a human, with a structured handoff.

questions.stem: Riverbend's human agents run their own identity checks before acting on an account. The support agent's verification gate is registered as `PreToolUse: [{ matcher: "apply_bill_credit|create_payment_plan|escalate_to_agent", hooks: [requireVerifiedCaller] }]` and denies each matched call until `verify_caller` has returned `{"verified": true}` in the session. Last month 212 callers failed `verify_caller` and then asked for a person, but every escalation was denied, and 61% of those chats ended with the customer leaving. How should the team change the gate?

options.text: Keep the hook and its matcher, but change the deny reason for `escalate_to_agent` so the gate tells the agent to offer every caller who asks another round of `verify_caller`.
options.explanation: It is the same hook with a friendlier reason, but callers who already failed are sent back to the check that stopped them, and their request for a person is still refused. Another round would suit a caller who mistyped an answer and hasn't asked for anyone.

options.text: Remove the gate that guards `apply_bill_credit` and `create_payment_plan`, and state in the system prompt that credits and plans need a verified caller but escalation does not.
options.explanation: Dropping the gate reopens transfers but turns the identity rule for credits and plans back into a request the model usually follows. Moving money for an unverified caller has to be blocked in code; a prompt rule suits guidance that can tolerate the odd miss.

options.text: Keep the hook, but narrow its matcher to `apply_bill_credit|create_payment_plan`, so credits and plans still wait for `verify_caller` while `escalate_to_agent` stays open to every caller who asks.
options.explanation: A gate should block the actions its rule protects, not the route to a person. Credits and plans still need a verified caller, but a transfer exposes nothing because human agents check identity themselves, so the 212 callers reach someone instead of leaving.

options.text: Keep the matcher, and have the agent take a callback number from unverified callers so the billing team can phone them after checking their identity.
options.explanation: A callback keeps the gate and promises a person, but hours later, and the billing team runs the same identity check it would run on a live transfer, so the delay buys nothing. Callbacks suit hours when no agent is free.

questions.keyConcept: Gate the actions a rule protects, not the route to a person; escalation stays open when humans run their own checks.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.5 (block and redirect to human escalation); §3 Task 1.4

questions.stem: Riverbend policy now says customers on the vulnerable-customer register may only be offered hardship payment plans. `create_payment_plan` writes the plan and sends the customer's plan letter in the same call. A `PostToolUse` hook on that tool enforces the policy, and last month's log holds 17 lines such as `additionalContext: "Account 40712 is on the register; cancel plan P-8841 and recreate it with plan_type=hardship"`. The agent recreated all 17 plans, yet each of those customers first received a standard-plan letter. Other plan requests must not slow down. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Keep the `PostToolUse` hook on `create_payment_plan`, but have it cancel non-hardship plans for register accounts and recreate them on hardship terms in code, not through the agent.
options.explanation: Doing the fix in code is deterministic, but it undoes the wrong plan after `create_payment_plan` has run, when the standard-plan letter has already gone out. A `PostToolUse` hook suits work on results; stopping a call with side effects needs the check before it.

options.text: Move the same check to a `PreToolUse` hook on `create_payment_plan` that denies non-hardship plans for register accounts and points the agent to hardship terms.
options.explanation: The letter is sent the moment the tool runs, so the check has to run before the call. A `PreToolUse` deny stops the standard plan for register customers before any letter exists, and its reason sends the agent straight to hardship terms; other plans pass through untouched.

options.text: State the hardship rule in the system prompt with two worked examples of register customers, and keep the `PostToolUse` hook on `create_payment_plan` as a backstop.
options.explanation: Examples would make standard plans for register customers rarer, not impossible, and the backstop still fires only after the letter is out. A prompt suits judgment calls; a letter that breaks policy has to be stopped before it is sent.

options.text: Hold plan letters from `create_payment_plan` for 24 hours, so the `PostToolUse` hook's cancellation lands before a letter reaches a register customer.
options.explanation: Holding letters would let the cancellation land first, but it delays the letter for every customer, which the stem rules out, and it still relies on the model acting on the hook's message. It works around the timing instead of checking before the call.

questions.keyConcept: When a tool's side effect happens as it runs, enforce the rule in a PreToolUse hook; a PostToolUse check is too late.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.5 (hooks on outgoing tool calls); §5 Key decision frameworks

questions.stem: Riverbend's `get_meter_reads` is defined as `{"name": "get_meter_reads", "description": "Returns meter reads.", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"meter_id": {"type": "string"}}}}`. In 18% of lookups the log shows a call such as `get_meter_reads({"meter_id": "4471-0093"}) → unknown meter_id`, where `4471-0093` is the account number from the `get_account` result fetched just before, though that same result lists the account's meters under `meters`, with IDs such as `E-0048213`. Which change fixes these calls?

options.text: Set `tool_choice` to force `get_account` before each `get_meter_reads` call, so the account details are in front of the agent when it builds `meter_id`.
options.explanation: Forcing a tool controls which tool runs, not what value goes into the next call. The log shows `get_account` was already fetched just before; the agent didn't know which field is the meter ID. Forcing suits a step that gets skipped.

options.text: Rewrite the description to list what `get_meter_reads` returns for each `meter_id`: dated reads from the last 24 months, newest first, and the account numbers they belong to.
options.explanation: A fuller description of the output is good practice, but these calls fail on the way in: the agent sends the wrong input. Describing returns would help if the agent picked the wrong tool, not when it fills the right tool's parameter with an account number.

options.text: Rewrite the description and the `meter_id` parameter description: IDs look like `E-0048213`, come from the `meters` list in `get_account`, and are never account numbers.
options.explanation: The agent passes the wrong value because the definition never says what a meter ID is. Stating the format, an example and where the ID comes from in the parameter description fixes the 18% at the source, since the definition is all the model sees of the tool.

options.text: Add a rule in capitals at the top of the system prompt: NEVER pass an account number to `get_meter_reads` as its `meter_id`.
options.explanation: It forbids the exact mistake in the log but doesn't supply the missing information, what a meter ID looks like or where to find one, so the agent is left guessing at another field. Format guidance belongs in the parameter description, which travels with the tool to every agent that loads it.

questions.keyConcept: When the agent passes a wrong value, fix the parameter description with its format, an example and where the value comes from.

questions.stem: Riverbend's 2,000-word system prompt has a policy section stating the $250 approval limit, and a `PreToolUse` hook denies any `apply_bill_credit` call above it. The tool's description, however, reads only "Applies a credit to a bill." In 22 of 140 reviewed outage chats the agent's reply promised a $300 credit in the same turn as the tool call; the hook denied the call, and the agent had to take the promise back. Rewording the policy section last month changed nothing. What is the best next step?

options.text: Add the $250 limit and the route above it, a call to `escalate_to_agent` for approval, to the `apply_bill_credit` description, and keep the same hook as enforcement.
options.explanation: The agent settles the amount while it is calling the tool, and the definition it reads then says nothing about a limit. Writing the boundary and the escalation route into the description puts them where the decision is made, and the hook still guarantees no credit above $250 goes through.

options.text: Make the hook's deny reason name the $250 limit and tell the agent to call `escalate_to_agent` for approval, and leave the description alone.
options.explanation: A clear deny reason helps the agent recover, but the reply promising $300 was written alongside the call, so the customer has already been told. It would be the fix if the trouble began after the denial, as with a generic "Blocked by policy" reason.

options.text: Add the $250 limit and the route above it to the `apply_bill_credit` description, and remove the hook, because the agent will know the limit before it offers.
options.explanation: The description change is right, but a description steers the model; it enforces nothing. Dropping the hook makes the approval rule depend on the model reading well on every call, and a money rule needs its guarantee kept in code.

options.text: Add a screening agent that reads each draft reply for credit amounts and holds any reply promising a credit above $250 until a person approves it.
options.explanation: A second agent screening every reply adds a model call and a delay to all chats to catch a gap that one sentence in the tool definition closes. A screening step would suit risky free text that no tool call reveals, not a known limit on one tool.

questions.keyConcept: Put a tool's boundaries in its description so the agent knows them when it decides; keep the hook for enforcement.

questions.stem: Riverbend's `create_payment_plan` accepts a `start_date` up to 30 days from today. For any later date it returns `{"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Operation failed"}], "isError": true}`, the same response it gives when the billing system is down. Many customers ask to start after their next payday, and 31% of plan requests now end in `escalate_to_agent`, although a customer offered a date inside the window usually takes it. What should `create_payment_plan` return for a start date beyond the window?

options.text: A business-rule error marked not retryable, with a customer-friendly note that plan start dates are set by Riverbend policy and need a person to change them.
options.explanation: A business-rule error with a note that a person must change the date tells the agent this is a policy refusal it cannot settle, so it keeps escalating chats the customer could finish by picking a date inside the window. A business error that needs a person would fit a request no date could satisfy, such as an account barred from plans.

options.text: A transient error marked retryable, with the note "Plan service busy, please retry", so the agent repeats the call with `start_date` unchanged a moment later.
options.explanation: Calling it transient sends the agent to repeat the exact call, which fails again because the date hasn't changed. Transient and retryable would fit the billing system being down, the other case that now returns "Operation failed".

options.text: A success result with `start_date` moved to the 30th day, so the plan is created on the spot without the agent stopping to ask the customer anything.
options.explanation: The customer gets a plan with a start date they never agreed to, and the agent doesn't know it was changed, so it may confirm the wrong date. A failure the agent can act on beats a success that hides one.

options.text: A validation error marked not retryable as sent, with a note naming `start_date` and its allowed range of up to 30 days for a corrected call.
options.explanation: The input is wrong, not the system: any date inside 30 days would succeed. Naming the field and the allowed range tells the agent what to ask the customer, and the call can then be made again with a corrected date, which keeps these chats out of the 31% that end with a person.

questions.keyConcept: A bad input should return a validation error naming the field and the allowed values, so the agent can correct the call and retry.

questions.stem: Riverbend resolves 71% of contacts without a person against its 75% target. Most of the gap is rare requests, such as direct-debit changes and meter-exchange bookings, that the agent escalates because it has no tool for them. Five of its tools, from `get_account` to `escalate_to_agent`, cover 92% of contacts. An engineer proposes giving the support agent all 19 billing API endpoints, but in a trial, wrong-tool picks on common requests rose from 2% to 9%. How should the architect respond to the proposal?

options.text: Accept the proposal, and give the support agent a detailed description with example requests for each of the 19 endpoints, such as direct-debit changes, so it can pick among them.
options.explanation: Good descriptions are worth having, but the trial already shows 19 tools on one agent raising wrong picks on common requests to 9%. Descriptions help an agent choose among a handful of tools; they don't remove the cost of a long list.

options.text: Keep the support agent on its five core tools, and add a billing-changes subagent with a few tools for the rare workflows, from direct-debit changes to meter-exchange bookings.
options.explanation: Selection gets worse as one agent's tool list grows, as the jump from 2% to 9% shows. Keeping five tools protects the 92% of common contacts, and a billing-changes subagent with a few tools built for the rare workflows lets those requests be resolved instead of escalated, closing the gap to 75%.

options.text: Decline the proposal, keep the support agent on its five core tools, and keep escalating the rare requests, such as direct-debit changes, to people.
options.explanation: It protects tool selection, but it leaves resolution at 71% against a 75% target, and the rare requests are where the gap is. Escalating rare requests would be fine if the agent were already meeting its target.

options.text: Accept the proposal, but name the rare endpoints with a `rare_` prefix, so the support agent reaches for them only after its five core tools.
options.explanation: A prefix changes names, not the number of choices: the agent still weighs 19 tools on each turn, and that load is what raised wrong picks to 9%. Renaming fixes overlap between two similar tools, not an overlong list.

questions.keyConcept: Keep each agent's tool list short; give rare capabilities to a scoped subagent instead of loading every endpoint onto one agent.

questions.stem: Riverbend's web-chat intake calls the Messages API directly with the support tools, and the chat widget puts the signed-in account number in the first message. In 9% of chats the model answers that message from the customer's own description of the bill, before calling `get_account`, and quotes a wrong balance. The system prompt already says to call `get_account` first. After that call most turns are plain explanations, though some later turns need `get_meter_reads`. Which `tool_choice` setup fixes this?

options.text: Set `tool_choice` to `"any"` on the first request of each chat, then `"auto"` for every later turn, so the opening reply must start with a tool call.
options.explanation: `"any"` guarantees some tool call on the first request but leaves the model to choose which, so it could open with `get_meter_reads` and still answer without the balance. `"any"` suits a step where any of several tools is acceptable.

options.text: Force `{"type": "tool", "name": "get_account"}` on every request in the chat, so the account data is reloaded before each reply the agent writes.
options.explanation: Forcing `get_account` on every request means no turn can end in a plain explanation or a `get_meter_reads` call, so the answers most turns need never arrive. Forcing suits only the step that must run first.

options.text: Force `{"type": "tool", "name": "get_account"}` on the first request of each chat, then use `"auto"` for every later turn, so a later reply can be plain text.
options.explanation: A forced tool choice guarantees `get_account` runs before the model writes anything on the first request, which removes the 9% of answers given without the account. Returning to `"auto"` lets later turns explain in text or call `get_meter_reads` when needed.

options.text: Keep `"auto"` throughout, and move the `get_account` rule to the top of the system prompt with an example of a first reply that calls it.
options.explanation: The prompt already says to call `get_account` first and 9% of chats still skip it; moving the rule up and adding an example may lower that, but `"auto"` still lets the model answer before calling. The guarantee has to come from the setting.

questions.keyConcept: To make one tool run first, force it by name on the first request only, then return tool_choice to auto.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.3 (forced tool_choice for the first step); §5 Key decision frameworks

questions.stem: Riverbend wants the agent to answer "why did my bills go up?" within the chat. Its prompt sets a fixed plan: starting from the oldest of the customer's last 24 electricity and water bills, run `get_meter_reads`, a tariff check and a usage comparison on each bill in turn until the rise is explained. These chats average about 40 tool calls, but 3 in 10 customers leave before the answer. `get_account` already lists each bill's total, usage and read type, and the largest bill is often a catch-up after months of estimated reads, explained by the smaller bills before it. Which two changes should the team make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Begin with the bill list from `get_account`, comparing totals, usage and read type across all 24 bills to see where the rise sits before calling any other tool.
options.explanation: An open-ended question starts with a cheap map of the whole picture. One `get_account` result already holds all 24 bills, so comparing them shows which months carry the rise and which are ordinary before any per-bill call is made, instead of spending about 40 calls working forward from the oldest bill.

options.text: Keep the three checks on each bill, but run them on the bills in order of their totals, largest first, until the rise is explained.
options.explanation: Ranking by total looks like a prioritised plan, but the checks and their order are still fixed up front. When the largest bill is a catch-up, its cause sits in the smaller estimated bills before it, which a largest-first order reaches only after every larger bill. A ranked fixed list would suit causes that sit inside the biggest bills themselves.

options.text: Choose each next check from the last finding: a high bill after estimated reads leads to the months before it, a tariff change to the bills after it.
options.explanation: An open-ended investigation should change its plan as findings come in. A catch-up bill is explained by the estimated months before it, so once a check shows estimated reads, those months are the next target; a plan fixed in advance keeps running the same checks on whatever bill comes next.

options.text: Hand these questions to a person with `escalate_to_agent`, passing the 24-bill list and the checks so far, since the investigation runs too long for the chat.
options.explanation: Escalating would end the long chats, but the answer needs only data the agent's own tools return and no credit or approval, so a person would run the same checks, and each handoff counts against the 75% target. Escalation fits a request for a person, a policy gap or a case where no progress is possible.

options.text: Run these investigations as an overnight Message Batches API job over the 24 bills, and email each customer the explanation the next morning.
options.explanation: An overnight batch removes the time pressure, but Riverbend wants the answer within the chat, and batch results can take up to 24 hours. A batch job suits work nobody is waiting on, such as a monthly review of billing anomalies.

questions.keyConcept: For open-ended investigations, map the whole picture cheaply first, then let each finding choose the next check instead of a fixed plan.

questions.stem: Riverbend's agent has a generic `update_account(field, value)` tool, added so it could change addresses. It accepts any of 60 field names, at least 9 of which change what a customer owes, and the billing team adds fields most quarters. Last month the agent set `credit_balance` directly in 5 chats, giving credits of up to $400 that the `PreToolUse` hook on `apply_bill_credit` never saw. Address, phone and email changes are 6% of contacts and must stay self-service. Which change closes the gap?

options.text: Keep `update_account`, and add a `PreToolUse` hook that denies calls to the 9 fields that change what a customer owes, so each balance change goes through `apply_bill_credit`.
options.explanation: It blocks today's 9 money fields at the right point, but it is a list someone must keep in step with a schema that grows most quarters, and the next new money field is open until someone notices. A blocklist suits a short, fixed set of dangerous inputs.

options.text: Keep `update_account`, and rewrite its description to say it takes address, phone and email alone, so a balance change can only go through `apply_bill_credit`.
options.explanation: A clearer description makes misuse less likely, but the tool can still write `credit_balance`, and credits up to $400 have already gone through it. Where money is involved, the tool's contract has to make the wrong call impossible, not unlikely.

options.text: Keep `update_account`, and route each of its calls through `escalate_to_agent`, so a person confirms each account change before it is written.
options.explanation: Each address change would wait for a person, though these are 6% of contacts and must stay self-service. Escalation suits decisions that need a human, not routine edits that a narrower tool can make safe.

options.text: Replace `update_account` with `update_contact_details`, which takes address, phone and email alone, so a balance change can only go through `apply_bill_credit` and its hook.
options.explanation: A tool that can write any field lets the agent route around the money controls. A purpose-built tool that accepts contact fields alone makes a balance change through it impossible, keeps address changes self-service, and holds however many fields billing adds later.

questions.keyConcept: Replace a generic tool that can reach dangerous fields with a constrained tool whose contract makes misuse impossible.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 2.3 (replace generic tools with constrained ones); §3 Task 1.5

questions.stem: Each turn, Riverbend's agent receives a 9,000-token account dump in stored order: tariff history, free-text notes, then 40 bills. The note "meter exchange booked for 14 March", added in early February, sits near the middle. In about 1 in 6 contacts like this the agent books a second exchange, or tells the customer estimated reads will go on indefinitely. The team already added "read every account note carefully" to the system prompt, and the rate barely moved. The full history must stay available for billing disputes. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Organise the dump under explicit section headers, with open bookings, open disputes and promised actions under a Notes header, and leave the order as it is.
options.explanation: Headers help the model find its way through the dump, but the booking note stays in the middle, where it is being missed. Headers are half of the fix; they work best below a short summary of the facts the agent must act on.

options.text: Start the dump with a key-facts block listing open bookings, open disputes and promised actions, and keep the full dump after it under section headers.
options.explanation: Models handle the start and end of a long input reliably and the middle less so, which is where the booking note sits. A key-facts block at the top puts open bookings and promises where they are read, and headers organise the rest, with the full history kept.

options.text: Move the agent to a model with a larger context window, so the 9,000-token dump takes up a smaller share of what the model can read on each turn.
options.explanation: The dump already fits easily; the problem is where the note sits, not how much room there is. A larger window doesn't change how the middle of a long input is processed, and it would suit inputs that are being cut off.

options.text: Send the 10 latest bills and the notes from the last two weeks, so the dump shrinks to about a quarter of its present size.
options.explanation: Trimming shrinks the dump, but it drops every bill and note outside those windows, and the full history must stay available for billing disputes. Trimming suits fields nobody uses, not history the team has to keep.

questions.keyConcept: Put a key-facts summary at the start of long aggregated inputs and organise the rest under headers to avoid lost-in-the-middle misses.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.1 (lost in the middle; key findings first, section headers)

questions.stem: Riverbend's agent summarises older turns once a chat passes 50,000 tokens. Each `get_meter_reads` result carries about 4,000 tokens of half-hourly data, though the agent uses only the read date, read type and value, so multi-bill chats reach that point within about 12 messages. After one summary, the agent called the $38.60 disputed on bill B-20931 "about $40" and offered a $62 credit on bill B-21407 that it had already applied. Summaries end well inside their output limit, and customers often refer back to what they said earlier. Which two changes should the team make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Keep a case-facts block of bill IDs, disputed amounts, dates and statuses, such as B-21407 credited $62, and send it with every request outside the summarised history.
options.explanation: Summarisation turns exact figures into vague text, so transactional facts belong in a case-facts block kept outside the summarised history and sent with each request. The $38.60 on B-20931 and the credit already applied to B-21407 then reach every turn unchanged, however often older turns are summarised.

options.text: Add a `PostToolUse` hook that cuts each `get_meter_reads` result down to the read date, read type and value before the agent sees it.
options.explanation: Tool results use tokens out of proportion to their relevance: about 4,000 tokens per read result, when the agent uses three fields. A `PostToolUse` hook can replace the output the model sees, so each lookup adds a small fraction of that, and chats reach the 50,000-token summary point far later.

options.text: Tell the summariser to copy every dollar amount, bill ID and credit status into each summary exactly as written in the chat.
options.explanation: An instruction makes exact copies more likely, but the summariser still rewrites the text and can blur a figure, as one summary already did with $38.60. Money figures that must stay exact belong outside the summary; a summariser instruction suits wording and emphasis.

options.text: At each summary point, drop the history and send only a case-facts block of bill IDs, amounts and statuses with the latest message.
options.explanation: Sending only the block keeps the figures, but it throws away the conversation the summary still holds, and customers often refer back to what they said earlier. The block is meant to sit beside the summarised history, not replace it; a clean start suits a new, unrelated request.

options.text: Raise the summariser's `max_tokens` so that each summary has room to keep every amount, bill ID, date and credit status from the chat.
options.explanation: `max_tokens` caps how long a summary may be, and these summaries already end well inside that limit, so the cap isn't what drops the figures. Raising it helps only when a summary is cut off at the limit.

questions.keyConcept: Keep exact case facts (amounts, dates, bill IDs, statuses) in a block outside the summarised history, sent with every request.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.1 (persistent case-facts block; trim tool outputs)

questions.stem: At Riverbend, credits above $250 go to a human approver through `escalate_to_agent`. For wrong-tariff disputes, the agent sends a tariff-review subagent through up to 36 bills, looking up the tariff record behind each. Its 1,500-word narratives crowded the agent's context in chats with several disputes, so the team capped them at 200 words, and context use is now fine. Since then, however, approvers have sent back 1 in 5 of these credit requests because they don't say which bills were on the wrong tariff or which tariff record shows it. Chats still often cover several disputes. What should the subagent return?

options.text: Fixed fields for each bill in the dispute: bill ID, period, tariff charged, tariff that should apply, overcharge, and the tariff record ID that shows it.
options.explanation: When downstream context is tight, upstream agents should return structured facts with their sources instead of prose. A few fixed fields per affected bill stay small in chats with several disputes, and every credit request can then name the bills on the wrong tariff and the record behind each, which is what approvers sent back 1 in 5 requests for lacking.

options.text: The uncapped 1,500-word narrative, placed first in the agent's next request under a "Tariff findings" header so each bill ID and tariff record ID stands out.
options.explanation: Key findings at the start under a clear header help a reader find them in a long input, which is why this tempts. But the full narrative is what crowded the agent's context in multi-dispute chats, and moving it to the front doesn't shrink it. Placement suits an input that already fits.

options.text: Its 200-word narrative as now, with the agent taking each bill ID and tariff record ID from the subagent's tool results when it writes to the approver.
options.explanation: Only a subagent's final message reaches the agent; the tariff records it looked up stay in its own context. With the 200-word narrative as the only output, the IDs approvers ask for never reach the agent. It would work only if the IDs were in that final message.

options.text: Its 1,500-word narrative passed to an extraction subagent, which pulls out each bill ID, period and tariff record ID and sends the agent a short list.
options.explanation: An extraction step would recover the IDs, but it adds an agent and a handoff for data the tariff-review subagent already holds, since it looked up each record. Changing its output format gives the same fields without the extra hop; a separate extractor suits output from a source you can't change.

questions.keyConcept: When downstream context is tight, have upstream agents return fixed fields with source references, not prose, even short prose.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.1 (upstream agents return structured data); §3 Task 1.3

questions.stem: A Riverbend product manager proposes escalating any contact where the sentiment score drops below -0.6 or the agent rates its own confidence under 0.7. A trial on 500 transcripts escalated many angry customers whose estimated-read questions the agent had already solved, but missed calm customers whose requests fall outside written policy, such as waiving the standing charge on an empty second home. The human queue must not grow. What should the team do instead?

options.text: Keep both scores, tune the tone cut-off to -0.8 and confidence to 0.5 on last month's transcripts, and add worked examples to the system prompt.
options.explanation: New cut-offs only trade one error for the other: a lower tone bar still escalates angry, solved cases, and a calm policy-gap request still scores well on both. Examples can't rescue a trigger that measures the wrong thing; tuning would suit a score that tracked the need for a person.

options.text: Add to the system prompt explicit triggers, a request for a person, a request outside written policy and no progress, each with its own worked example.
options.explanation: Tone and self-rated confidence don't track whether a case needs a person: the trial escalated solved angry cases and missed calm policy gaps. Named triggers with examples point the agent at the real conditions, so policy gaps reach people and routine cases don't, keeping the queue flat.

options.text: Train a separate escalation classifier on past transcripts that people escalated, and run it on each turn of the chat to decide whether to call `escalate_to_agent`.
options.explanation: A classifier adds a model call on each turn and a component to maintain, for a judgment that explicit criteria with examples can guide, and past escalations may carry the same tone-driven habit. A classifier would suit routing among many queues, not three named triggers.

options.text: Drop both scores, and add to the system prompt one explicit trigger, a request for a person, leaving the other contacts for the agent to resolve.
options.explanation: An explicit request is one real trigger, but not the only one: calm customers asking for something outside written policy would still be handled alone, which was the trial's second failure. Policy gaps and lack of progress need to escalate too.

questions.keyConcept: Escalate on explicit triggers with examples, a request for a person, a policy gap, no progress, not on sentiment or self-rated confidence.

questions.stem: A Riverbend customer writes: "This is ridiculous. You've taken my direct debit twice this month and now I'm overdrawn!" The duplicate payment is $96, and the agent can return it at once as a credit with `apply_bill_credit`. The customer hasn't asked for a person, but the agent now escalates every message that reads as angry, and these chats wait about 40 minutes in the human queue. How should the agent respond to messages like this?

options.text: Acknowledge the frustration, and call `escalate_to_agent` straight away with the duplicate payment details, so a person can return the $96.
options.explanation: Anger isn't a reason to hand over a $96 credit the agent can make itself; the customer would wait about 40 minutes for something one call solves. Escalating straight away is right when the customer asks for a person.

options.text: Acknowledge the frustration, offer to credit the $96 now, and call `escalate_to_agent` if the customer's messages stay negative across the next two.
options.explanation: It resolves first, which is right, but it escalates on tone: a customer still annoyed about being overdrawn may be content with the fix, and a calm one who asks for a person would be missed. The trigger should be the request, not the sentiment.

options.text: Credit the $96 now, and if the customer still asks for a person, explain that the refund is done and close the chat.
options.explanation: Fixing the payment is right, but an explicit request for a person has to be honoured even when the agent thinks the issue is solved. Closing the chat on that request ignores the clearest escalation trigger there is.

options.text: Acknowledge the frustration, offer to credit the $96 now, and call `escalate_to_agent` if the customer then asks for a person.
options.explanation: The issue is simple and within the agent's authority, and the customer hasn't asked for a person. Acknowledging the frustration and fixing the $96 now resolves it in the chat instead of a 40-minute wait, and a request for a person, if it comes, is honoured straight away.

questions.keyConcept: With a frustrated customer and a simple issue, acknowledge, offer the fix, and escalate when the customer asks for a person.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 5.2 (acknowledge and offer to resolve); §5 Key decision frameworks

questions.stem: Ironpine's gameplay team committed a project subagent, `lua-perf`, that profiles `gameplay/` scripts and returns the five slowest functions with their cost per frame. Most Lua requests at the studio are small edits that need no profiling. The subagent's frontmatter reads `name: lua-perf` and `description: Lua helper`, and its 40-line prompt sets out the profiling steps. Last month engineers asked about frame-time spikes in gameplay scripts 60 times, and Claude delegated to `lua-perf` only twice, profiling inline in the main conversation the other times. What should the team change?

options.text: Add a line to the project `CLAUDE.md` telling Claude to always use `lua-perf` for Lua work in gameplay scripts, from frame-time spikes to small edits.
options.explanation: A standing rule to hand all `gameplay/` Lua work to `lua-perf` would launch a profiling run for the many small edits too, adding time and cost to each. A CLAUDE.md line suits a project-wide convention; when to use one subagent belongs in that subagent's description.

options.text: Rewrite the `description` to say when to use it, for all frame-time spikes in gameplay scripts, and what it returns to Claude.
options.explanation: The main agent picks a subagent by reading its description, and `Lua helper` gives it no reason to choose `lua-perf` for a frame-time spike. A description that names the trigger and the result lets Claude delegate on the 60 spike requests and leave small edits alone.

options.text: Expand the 40-line prompt into a clearer step-by-step profiling sequence with a fixed output format for the five slowest Lua functions.
options.explanation: The prompt is what the subagent works from, which matters only after it has been launched. Claude chose not to launch it in 58 of 60 cases, so a better procedure changes nothing there. A defined output format would be the right next step once delegation works.

options.text: Add a `PreToolUse` hook that blocks `Read` on Lua files in `gameplay/` in the main session until `lua-perf` has run in that conversation.
options.explanation: A hook suits a rule that must hold without exception, and this is a routing judgment. Blocking each `Read` on gameplay Lua until a profile has run would also stall the small edits that need no profiling, while the vague description stays the cause.

questions.keyConcept: The main agent decides when to launch a subagent from its description, so the description must say when to use it and what it returns.

questions.stem: Ironpine's `/review-pr` command runs a separate pass on each changed file; each pass is given only that file's diff and has no search tools. Last quarter those passes caught 31 local defects such as leaks and missing null checks. A recent PR changed the binding `Spawn(entity, pos)` in `engine/script/bindings.cpp` to `Spawn(entity, pos, layer)`. Every per-file pass approved, but 14 Lua callers in `gameplay/`, none of them in the PR, still passed two arguments and crashed in QA. An engineer proposes replacing the per-file passes with one review of the whole 40-file diff. Which two should the review design include? (Select 2.)

options.text: Replace the per-file passes with one review of the whole 40-file diff in a single prompt, so each file is read alongside the others.
options.explanation: One prompt over 40 files spreads attention thin, so the local defects the per-file passes catch start to slip. It would not have caught this bug either: the 14 Lua callers were not in the diff. A single pass suits a small diff, not this one.

options.text: Keep the per-file passes for local defects in each changed file, as they already catch leaks and missing null checks reliably.
options.explanation: Per-file passes give each file focused attention, which is why they found 31 local defects. The miss was a cross-file problem, so replacing them would trade a working check for nothing. They stay as the first stage of the review chain.

options.text: Add to each per-file pass an instruction to confirm that callers elsewhere in the repository still match every function the file changes.
options.explanation: Each per-file pass is given only its own file's diff and has no search tools, so it cannot find the callers elsewhere to confirm they still match. At most it could notice that a signature changed. Checking the call sites needs a step that can search the repository and see the signature and the callers together.

options.text: Run each per-file pass twice, with two independent reviewer instances, and keep only the findings that both of the instances report.
options.explanation: A second independent instance gives each file a fresh look, which helps when a reviewer is biased by its own work. Here both instances still get only one file's diff and no search tools, so neither could see the stale Lua callers, and the cost doubles.

options.text: Add a cross-file integration pass, with search across the repository, that lists each changed binding signature in `engine/script/` and checks every Lua call site in `gameplay/` against it.
options.explanation: The stale callers were outside the changed file, and outside the diff. An integration pass that can search the repository, takes each changed binding signature and checks its Lua call sites in `gameplay/` is the step built for that, and it would have flagged the 14 two-argument calls.

questions.keyConcept: Large reviews keep focused per-file passes for local defects and add an integration pass for problems that cross file boundaries.
questions.studyRef: §3 Task 1.6; §5 Patterns in the correct answers

questions.stem: Ironpine's root `CLAUDE.md` contains the line `Indent with tabs everywhere.`, and `engine/CLAUDE.md` contains `Indent C++ with 4 spaces.` The engineer who wrote the engine file expected it to replace the root file for engine work, but about a third of Claude's engine edits use tabs and some files now mix both. He moved the engine line to the top of its file and prefixed it with `IMPORTANT:`, yet the mixing continued. Gameplay and tools code must keep tabs. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Move `Indent C++ with 4 spaces.` into a `.claude/rules/engine-style.md` file scoped to `engine/**`, so only engine edits load the engine rule.
options.explanation: A scoped rule loads only for engine files, but the root file still loads with `tabs everywhere`, so engine edits still carry both instructions. Moving the engine rule changes when it loads, not the conflict. A scoped rule would suit an engine convention with no rival rule in the root.

options.text: Delete the root rule `Indent with tabs everywhere.` and have gameplay and tools engineers keep it in their own `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` files.
options.explanation: This removes the conflict but turns a team convention into personal files. Each gameplay and tools engineer, and each monthly new hire, would need to add the line, and anyone who skips it gets no tab rule. User-level files suit personal preferences, not studio standards.

options.text: Reword the root rule to `Indent with tabs in gameplay/ and tools/.` and keep the engine file's rule as the only one for engine code.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md files do not override each other: the root and engine files load together and their text is concatenated. With `tabs everywhere` still in the root, engine sessions carry two rules that contradict. Scoping the root rule to `gameplay/` and `tools/` removes the conflict and leaves the engine file's 4-space rule unopposed.

options.text: Copy the root file's other studio rules into `engine/CLAUDE.md`, leaving out the tab rule, so the engine file can stand in for the root file.
options.explanation: This rests on the same misreading that caused the problem: that the engine file replaces the root file. The root file still loads with its tab rule, so the copy only adds duplicated text that can drift. A standalone file would help only if files overrode each other.

questions.keyConcept: CLAUDE.md files at different levels stack rather than override, so rules that conflict must be rescoped until they no longer contradict.
questions.authorNote: Stacking (concatenation, not override) is listed in research §7 as beyond the guide; backed by d3 notes [MEM] [AC-CMDF].

questions.stem: A tools engineer at Ironpine says Claude ignores `tools/CLAUDE.md`: in her sessions it runs build scripts without the `--dry-run` flag that file requires, while two teammates say the same file works for them. Several people want to start rewriting the file, but the team lead first wants to know which memory files her session has actually loaded. What should she do first?

options.text: Ask Claude, in the session where the problem shows, to list the memory files it has loaded, and check whether `tools/CLAUDE.md` appears in its reply.
options.explanation: Claude's account of which files it loaded is its own explanation, not a record of what is in context, so it can be wrong in either direction. It sounds like the most direct check, but `/memory` gives the actual list.

options.text: Run `/init` so that Claude proposes a fresh starting CLAUDE.md, then compare it with `tools/CLAUDE.md` to see whether the `--dry-run` rule is the problem.
options.explanation: `/init` produces a starting CLAUDE.md; it says nothing about which memory files her session loaded, which is what the lead wants to know first. Comparing wording also looks for the cause in a file that already works for two teammates. `/init` suits a project that has no CLAUDE.md yet.

options.text: Copy the rules from `tools/CLAUDE.md` into the root `CLAUDE.md`, so they load at launch whichever directory her session starts in.
options.explanation: Copying the rules edits a shared file before the cause is known, and loads the tools rules in every engine and gameplay session. If the cause is something else, the change only adds clutter for 45 engineers.

options.text: Run `/memory` in the session where the problem shows, and check whether `tools/CLAUDE.md` appears among the memory files that session has loaded.
options.explanation: `/memory` lists the CLAUDE.md and other memory files loaded in the session, which is what the lead wants to know before anything is edited. If `tools/CLAUDE.md` is missing, the cause is loading; if it is listed, the cause is in what the rule says.

questions.keyConcept: When a CLAUDE.md file seems ignored, check which memory files the session has loaded with `/memory` before editing any file.

questions.stem: QA's 2,000-token console-certification checklist is pasted into both `engine/CLAUDE.md` and `tools/packager/CLAUDE.md`, the two areas whose code goes into certification builds. QA updated the engine copy twice this year but forgot the packager copy once, so the two now disagree on save-data rules. Gameplay work and the rest of `tools/` never need the checklist, and the gameplay team watches its context use closely. What should QA change?

options.text: Move the checklist to `docs/cert/checklist.md` and replace each pasted copy with an `@` import of that same file, relative to each directory file.
options.explanation: An `@` import pulls one file into each directory CLAUDE.md, so QA edits a single checklist and both areas get the change. Each directory file loads only when Claude works in its subtree, and the import loads with it, so gameplay sessions never carry the 2,000 tokens.

options.text: Move the checklist to `docs/cert/checklist.md`, import it once from the root `CLAUDE.md`, and delete the pasted copies from both directory files.
options.explanation: This gives one copy, but an import in the root file loads up front in every session, so all gameplay and other tools work carries the 2,000-token checklist. A root import suits guidance that every session needs.

options.text: Keep both pasted copies and add a CI check that fails any pull request in which the two checklist sections are no longer identical.
options.explanation: A CI job that polices two copies is extra machinery where one shared file would do: QA still edits both copies, and each update needs two matching changes. A check like this suits copies that cannot be shared, such as generated files.

options.text: Move the checklist into each QA engineer's `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`, so the QA team owns one version and updates it in a single place.
options.explanation: User-level files apply only to their owner and are not shared through git, so engine and packager engineers would stop getting the checklist at all. QA would also end up with one copy per QA engineer, not one for the studio.

questions.keyConcept: Use `@` imports to pull one shared standards file into each directory CLAUDE.md that needs it, instead of pasting copies.

questions.stem: A senior engine engineer wrote `/perf-capture`, which records a 300-frame GPU capture on the devkit and summarises the slowest render passes. It lives in her `~/.claude/commands/perf-capture.md`, and teammates who copied it from her by hand now run three different versions. The studio wants all 45 engineers, and the new hires who join each month, to get one version without any per-person setup, though most engineers take a capture only a few times a year. Where should the command live?

options.text: In each engineer's `~/.claude/commands/perf-capture.md`, copied from one file committed to git, so every engineer has the same `/perf-capture` after the copy.
options.explanation: A committed source file still leaves a copy step for each person, which is how the three versions arose. New hires who skip the step miss the command, and each later edit has to be copied again by each engineer. User-level commands suit a tool one person keeps for herself.

options.text: In the project `CLAUDE.md`, committed to git, as a section listing the capture steps for Claude to run when someone asks for a perf capture.
options.explanation: A CLAUDE.md section loads into every session for all 45 engineers, though most rarely take a capture, and it adds no `/perf-capture` command to invoke. CLAUDE.md suits standards that apply to all work; on-demand procedures belong in commands or skills.

options.text: In the project's `.claude/commands/perf-capture.md`, committed to git, so each clone gets the same `/perf-capture` and later edits reach engineers on their next pull.
options.explanation: Project commands in `.claude/commands/` are shared through version control, so everyone who clones the repository has `/perf-capture`, and an edit reaches all 45 engineers on their next pull. That ends the three hand-copied versions and needs no step from new hires.

options.text: In a small MCP server registered in the project `.mcp.json` that exposes a `perf_capture` tool, so each clone can run the capture.
options.explanation: Rebuilding a working prompt command as a server is more to build and maintain, when the only problem is where the file lives. An MCP server suits access to an external system that Claude has no other way to reach.

questions.keyConcept: A command the whole team needs goes in the committed `.claude/commands/` folder, not in one engineer's `~/.claude/commands/`.

questions.stem: Ironpine's project skill `.claude/skills/shader-test/SKILL.md` generates one regression test per shader. For her own deep reviews, a rendering engineer wants a version that also runs a precision sweep and writes a register-pressure report. For normal reviews she still runs the team's `/shader-test` as it is, and her 44 teammates must see no change to the shared skill. How should she set this up?

options.text: Copy the skill to `~/.claude/skills/shader-test/SKILL.md` and add her two steps, keeping the team's name so her command doesn't change.
options.explanation: Her personal folder is the right place for a variant, but the name does more than set her command: for the same name the personal layer outranks the project layer, so `/shader-test` would always run her deep version and the team's version could no longer be run for her normal reviews. Keeping the name suits a version meant to replace the team's every time.

options.text: Create `~/.claude/skills/shader-test-deep/SKILL.md` with the frontmatter `extends: shader-test` and only her two extra steps in the body, so it reuses the team's procedure.
options.explanation: `extends` is not a skill frontmatter field, so the file would hold only her two steps with no base procedure to run. A personal variant is a full copy of the skill under its own name.

options.text: Add her two steps to her `CLAUDE.local.md`, with a note to run them each time the shader-test skill runs, so teammates do not see them.
options.explanation: `CLAUDE.local.md` is personal, but it loads in each of her sessions in the repository, so the extra steps would apply to her normal reviews too. It fits personal instructions for all her work in one repository, not a variant she calls only sometimes.

options.text: Copy the skill to `~/.claude/skills/shader-test-deep/SKILL.md`, set its `name` to `shader-test-deep`, add her two steps, and run `/shader-test-deep` for deep reviews.
options.explanation: A personal skill in `~/.claude/skills/` is available only to her, and the frontmatter `name`, when set, becomes the command, so a copy that kept `name: shader-test` would still answer to the old name. The new name is what lets both skills exist side by side: `/shader-test-deep` for deep reviews, `/shader-test` for the team's version. The project file is untouched, so teammates see no change.

questions.keyConcept: Personal variants of a team skill go in `~/.claude/skills/` under a different name, so both versions stay callable.

questions.stem: Ironpine's `.claude/rules/cpp-memory.md` holds 60 lines on allocators and RAII for the C++ in `engine/` and in the native packer under `tools/packager/`. Its frontmatter reads `globs: ["engine/**/*.cpp", "tools/packager/**/*.cpp"]`. Gameplay engineers working only on Lua report that Claude brings up the allocator rules from the first prompt of a session, before it has opened any file. The convention must keep covering both C++ trees. What is the cause, and what is the fix?

options.text: A rule cannot cover two directory trees; move the 60 lines into `engine/CLAUDE.md`, which loads only when Claude works on files under `engine/`.
options.explanation: A rule can list patterns in several trees, so the cause is wrong, and `engine/CLAUDE.md` would miss the C++ under `tools/packager/`. A directory file suits a convention that belongs to one tree.

options.text: The two `globs` patterns are too narrow to match reliably; keep the key and merge both patterns into `**/*.cpp`, so any C++ file matches.
options.explanation: The patterns were never applied, because the key that holds them is ignored. Any pattern under `globs`, broad or narrow, leaves the file loading at launch. A broader pattern would be right only if a working `paths` key matched too few files.

options.text: A rule reads only `paths`, so `globs` is ignored and the file loads at launch; rename the key to `paths`, keeping both patterns.
options.explanation: Rules read only the `paths` frontmatter key. With `globs`, the file has no scope and loads at launch like the project CLAUDE.md, which is why Lua sessions see it from the first prompt. Renaming the key keeps both C++ patterns and makes the rule load only for matching files.

options.text: Files at the top level of `.claude/rules/` load at launch; move this one into a `.claude/rules/cpp/` subfolder so it is read only for C++ work.
options.explanation: Every `.md` file under `.claude/rules/` is discovered, subfolders included, so moving the file changes nothing about when it loads. Subfolders organize rules; only `paths` makes a rule conditional.

questions.keyConcept: A `.claude/rules/` file is path-scoped only through its `paths` key; a rule without one loads at launch in every session.

questions.stem: QA traced a devkit crash at Ironpine to `Mixer::SetChannelVolume` in `engine/audio/Mixer.cpp`: it indexes a gain table with the volume it receives, and some gameplay scripts pass values above 1.0. The audio lead has decided the fix, a clamp to the 0.0–1.0 range at the top of that function, and the existing audio unit tests cover it. The change is about three lines, but engine code falls under console certification, and a teammate suggests plan mode for any change in `engine/`. How should the engineer make the change with Claude Code?

options.text: Direct execution: give Claude the file, the function and the clamp to add, then read the diff and run the audio unit tests before committing.
options.explanation: Direct execution fits a simple, well-scoped change: one function in one file, with the fix already decided and tests that cover it. Naming the file, function and clamp keeps Claude from exploring, and reading the three-line diff and running the tests gives the certification code a real check.

options.text: Plan mode: have Claude read `engine/audio/` and propose a plan for the clamp, approve the plan, then let it edit `Mixer.cpp` and run the tests.
options.explanation: Plan mode suits large changes, several valid approaches, architectural decisions and multi-file changes. Here the lead has already chosen one fix in one function, so the plan would only restate a decided three-line clamp. Certification calls for a careful look at the change, which reading the diff gives.

options.text: An Explore subagent first: have it trace the callers of `SetChannelVolume` in `gameplay/` and `engine/`, then make the clamp by direct execution.
options.explanation: An Explore subagent isolates verbose discovery, but the clamp sits inside the function, so it covers every caller whatever value it passes. Tracing callers across two directories adds a step with nothing left to find. It would suit a crash whose cause had not yet been traced.

options.text: Direct execution, then ask Claude in that session to review its own diff against the certification rules instead of reading it.
options.explanation: Direct execution is right, but the session that wrote a change is not the best judge of it, because it reviews with the same reasoning that produced it. For certification code the check should be independent: the engineer reading the diff, or a review from a clean context.

questions.keyConcept: Use direct execution for a decided, single-file change; plan mode is for large, multi-file or open design work.

questions.stem: Ironpine's QA reports that about 1 in 50 controller button presses is lost during scene transitions. Each press passes through three subsystems: the device layer in `engine/input/`, the focus stack in `engine/ui/`, and the Lua bindings in `gameplay/input/`, and the team has not traced which one drops it. The lead expects the fix to be one line once the cause is found, but the patch must make Friday's build. Which two steps should the engineer take with Claude? (Select 2.)

options.text: Start in direct execution and add a guard against dropped events in each of the three subsystems, so whichever one loses the press is covered.
options.explanation: Guards in all three subsystems change code before the cause is known, and at least two of them patch places that are not at fault. A guard can also hide the real drop instead of fixing it.

options.text: Start in plan mode and have Claude trace a button press through all three subsystems to find where it is dropped, with no edits yet.
options.explanation: Where the event is lost is still open across three subsystems, and plan mode lets Claude read and trace the code without editing anything. The trace turns an unclear bug into a known one-line change.

options.text: After the cause is found, stay in plan mode and have Claude plan a rework of event queuing across all three subsystems before any fix.
options.explanation: A rework of event queuing across three subsystems is an architectural change, and the bug needs one line. Planning it would put Friday's build at risk for a design nobody asked for.

options.text: After the trace, open a new session for the fix and describe the lost-input bug to Claude from the QA report.
options.explanation: A new session throws away the trace that found the cause, so Claude would have to work it out from the QA report a second time. Continuing in the same session keeps the findings for the fix.

options.text: Once the cause is confirmed, leave plan mode and have Claude apply the one-line fix by direct execution, then review the diff.
options.explanation: Once the cause is confirmed the change is small and well understood, which is when direct execution fits. Leaving plan mode for the one-line fix and reviewing the diff gets the patch into Friday's build without another planning round.

questions.keyConcept: When the cause is unclear but the fix will be small, investigate in plan mode, then implement by direct execution.

questions.stem: A new Ironpine hire who came from web development is writing trophy-unlock code for the console builds. Console certification has trophy rules she has never worked with, though she knows the game's save code well. Her first prompt, "add trophy unlocks for the 12 story chapters", produced code that QA rejected for two requirements she had not known about. Certification submission is in three weeks, and each failed submission costs the studio a resubmission slot. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Give Claude two or three input and output examples of chapter-complete events and the unlock calls each one should produce, taken from QA's rejections.
options.explanation: Examples clarify a transformation whose requirements are known but read inconsistently. Here some requirements are unknown, and examples built from QA's two rejections can only teach those two.

options.text: Write tests first for the two requirements QA named, then have Claude write the code from them, sharing each failing test until it passes.
options.explanation: Tests first is the right loop once the requirements are known. Built from QA's two findings, the suite would pass while requirements nobody has named stay missing, so the next rejection would come from certification.

options.text: Ask Claude to interview her about the feature before any more code, then write the answers into a spec it builds from.
options.explanation: In an unfamiliar domain the gaps are things she does not know to ask about. Having Claude interview her surfaces considerations she would not think to raise before code is written, and the spec gives the implementation a full set of requirements instead of the two QA happened to find.

options.text: Rewrite the prompt as "add trophy unlocks that meet all console certification requirements" and have Claude regenerate the code from scratch.
options.explanation: A broader instruction leaves Claude to guess what certification requires, which is how the first draft went wrong. Nothing in it names the specific considerations, so the gaps stay hidden until QA or certification finds them.

questions.keyConcept: In an unfamiliar domain, have Claude interview you to surface requirements before it builds, then work from the resulting spec.

questions.stem: Ironpine's nightly CI job runs `claude -p --bare "Generate tests for changed files in tools/"`, a command copied from a lint job that uses `--bare` so every runner starts the same. `tools/CLAUDE.md` documents the testing standards and the shared fixtures `asset_tree` and `fake_devkit`, but over two weeks 70% of the generated tests built their own temporary asset folders instead of using `asset_tree`, and 40% repeated cases already in `tools/tests/`. Which two changes should the team make? (Select 2.)

options.text: Keep `--bare` and move the fixture notes from `tools/CLAUDE.md` into the root `CLAUDE.md`, so they load from the top of the project.
options.explanation: `--bare` skips CLAUDE.md files, the root one included, so moving the notes leaves them just as invisible to the job. It also puts tools-only text into each engineer's sessions. The move would help only a run that loads the root file but not `tools/CLAUDE.md`.

options.text: Remove `--bare` from the command, so the job reads `tools/CLAUDE.md` and the fixture notes in it when it opens files in `tools/`.
options.explanation: `--bare` skips CLAUDE.md files, hooks, skills, plugins and MCP discovery, so the job never sees the fixtures and standards in `tools/CLAUDE.md`. Without it, `-p` loads the same context as an interactive session, and the 70% of tests that built their own folders can use `asset_tree` instead.

options.text: Add `--output-format json` with a `--json-schema` that has `fixture` and `test_name` fields, so each generated test reports which fixture it uses.
options.explanation: A schema controls the shape of the output, so each test could report a `fixture` value, but the job still does not know `asset_tree` exists or which cases are covered. Structured output suits a pipeline that has to parse findings.

options.text: Put into the prompt the existing tests for each changed module in `tools/tests/`, so Claude adds only cases those tests do not cover.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md can say which fixtures exist, but not which cases the current tests cover. Giving Claude the existing tests for each changed module lets it add only missing cases, which targets the 40% that repeated `tools/tests/`.

options.text: Add a step that resumes the generating session with `--resume` and has it delete any of its tests it judges redundant.
options.explanation: A resumed session keeps the generator's own context, and that context still lacks the existing tests and the fixtures, so it has nothing to judge duplicates against. The session that wrote the tests is also not the best judge of them.

questions.keyConcept: CI runs need the project's CLAUDE.md for standards and fixtures, and the existing tests in context to avoid duplicate suggestions.
questions.authorNote: `--bare` is a CLI flag beyond the guide; its effect (skips CLAUDE.md, hooks, skills, plugins, MCP discovery) is in d3 notes [HEADLESS] [AC-HEADLESS].

questions.stem: Ironpine's root `CLAUDE.md` imports `@docs/style/lua.md`, a 3,000-token Lua style guide, so every session carries it, though most of the 45 engineers work only in C++. Lua lives in `gameplay/`, in `tools/lua/`, and in `engine/script/`, where the Lua glue sits beside 20 C++ binding files that engine engineers edit daily. A lead proposes moving the import into `gameplay/CLAUDE.md`, `tools/lua/CLAUDE.md` and `engine/script/CLAUDE.md` instead. How should you respond to the proposal?

options.text: Accept it: the three directory files load only for work in their trees, so all Lua work gets the guide and other C++ work skips it.
options.explanation: The three directory files load when Claude works on any file in their trees, and `engine/script/` holds 20 C++ binding files edited daily. Those C++ sessions would keep loading the 3,000-token guide. A directory file suits a convention that covers every file in one tree.

options.text: Decline it: keep only the `gameplay/CLAUDE.md` import, where most Lua is written, and leave Lua in the other two trees without the guide.
options.explanation: This saves the most tokens for C++ work, but Lua edits in `engine/script/` and `tools/lua/` would lose the style guide. It would fit only if all the studio's Lua lived under `gameplay/`.

options.text: Decline it: keep the root import and add a line telling Claude to set the Lua guide aside unless the task involves `.lua` files.
options.explanation: An import loads up front with the file that imports it, so the root import still puts 3,000 tokens into every session. A line asking Claude to set the text aside does not take it out of context; the C++ sessions pay the same as now.

options.text: Decline it: move the guide into `.claude/rules/lua-style.md` scoped in its frontmatter to `**/*.lua`, so it loads for every Lua file and nothing else.
options.explanation: A path-scoped rule loads only when Claude works with a matching file, so `**/*.lua` brings the guide in for Lua in all three trees and nowhere else. C++ binding work in `engine/script/` stays free of it, and the guide stays one committed file.

questions.keyConcept: A convention that follows one file type across mixed directories belongs in a path-scoped rule, not in directory CLAUDE.md files.

questions.stem: An Ironpine engineer had Claude build a cache for pathfinding queries in `engine/ai/`. Following team practice, she wrote the test suite first, covering normal paths, blocked tiles and invalidation when the map changes, and iterated by sharing failures until all 38 tests passed. On the devkit the cache takes 1.4 ms per frame in the 200-agent benchmark scene, but the console budget is 0.5 ms. The cache must keep passing the 38 tests. What should she do next?

options.text: Add the 0.5 ms budget to `engine/CLAUDE.md` as a standing rule, then ask Claude to optimise the cache and rerun the 38 tests.
options.explanation: A standing note makes Claude aware of the budget, but nothing measures whether a change meets it, and the 38 tests would pass at 1.4 ms just as they do now. A CLAUDE.md line suits a convention that review can check by eye.

options.text: Switch to plan mode, have Claude compare three cache designs for speed, and rebuild the cache from the chosen design before rerunning the 38 tests.
options.explanation: Redesigning throws away a cache that already passes 38 tests, and without a performance test the new design is no better measured than the old one. Comparing designs in plan mode suits an open architectural choice made before code exists.

options.text: Add a performance test that runs the 200-agent benchmark scene and fails above 0.5 ms per frame, then iterate by sharing its failures with Claude.
options.explanation: The suite covered behaviour and edge cases but not performance, so 1.4 ms passed every check. A test that fails above 0.5 ms in the benchmark scene turns the budget into a pass-or-fail check, and sharing its failures lets Claude iterate while the 38 tests guard correctness.

options.text: Ask Claude to optimise the cache, then add a performance test for the 200-agent benchmark scene whose expected frame time is what the optimised cache measures.
options.explanation: A test whose expected value comes from the optimised code records whatever time that code gets, even 1.4 ms, so it passes by definition. The test must state the 0.5 ms budget before the work, like the other 38.

questions.keyConcept: Test-first iteration covers performance requirements as well as behaviour and edge cases, so a budget becomes a pass-or-fail check.

questions.stem: An Ironpine engineer is two hours into a session moving `engine/save/` to a new save format, and she must keep working in it: it holds her plan and the decisions made so far, such as keeping version 3 saves readable. Before changing `SaveSlot::Write`, she needs every caller of it in the repository, with file and line, and the save versions `tools/savetool/` can still read. In last week's session, a similar question had Claude open 35 files, after which its answers spoke of "typical save systems" rather than the decisions made. How should she get the two answers?

options.text: Send each question to its own subagent, prompted with the question itself, like "list every caller of `SaveSlot::Write` with file and line", so only answers return.
options.explanation: A subagent runs in its own context window, so the file reading for each question stays there and only a short answer comes back. A specific prompt per question keeps the session that holds her plan and decisions free of the kind of 35-file reading that blurred last week's answers.

options.text: Send both questions to a subagent prompted "find what the refactor in progress needs around `SaveSlot::Write`", so it uses this session's plan and only the answers return.
options.explanation: A standard subagent starts fresh: it sees only the prompt it is given, not the plan or decisions in her session. "The refactor in progress" points at nothing it can read, so it has to guess what matters and explores broadly. Delegation works when the prompt itself states the questions, which she already has.

options.text: Ask both questions in this session, then run `/compact` with an instruction to keep the plan, the decisions and the two answers it found.
options.explanation: `/compact` helps once discovery output has already filled a session. Here the reading hasn't happened yet: asking in the session puts the raw file text in first, and compaction then summarises her plan and decisions along with it, which can lose details. A subagent keeps that text out from the start.

options.text: Run `/clear`, ask both questions in the emptied session, then re-explain the plan and the decisions to Claude from her own notes of the work.
options.explanation: `/clear` removes everything in the session, the plan and decisions she must keep working from included, and re-explaining them from notes rebuilds only part of two hours of work. `/clear` suits moving on to unrelated work.

questions.keyConcept: Send each specific discovery question to its own subagent, so the reading stays in its context and only the answer returns.

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's nightly test-generation job runs a custom loop on the Claude API, with `write_test_file` and `run_tests` as tools. The prompt asks Claude to say ALL TESTS WRITTEN when it has finished, and after running the requested tools the loop checks `if "ALL TESTS WRITTEN" in text: break`. In 14% of runs the job stops after one file, because Claude's first response restates its plan, phrase included, while also requesting `write_test_file`. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Loop again while the response holds a `tool_use` block, and finish the job only when Claude's text contains a rarer marker such as `<<TESTS_DONE>>`.
options.explanation: Continuing while a `tool_use` block is present is right, but finishing still depends on words Claude writes: a run that ends its turn without the marker has no clean stop, and Claude can quote the marker early. `"end_turn"` already says the work is done; a text marker is not a reliable signal.

options.text: Remove the text check and end the loop after 25 iterations, the most rounds any service has needed in the past month of nightly runs.
options.explanation: A cap of 25 would cut off a large service that needs more rounds, and it would keep calling the API after Claude has finished on a small one. A cap belongs in the loop only as a backstop behind `stop_reason`, not as the main rule for stopping.

options.text: Check `stop_reason` after every response: run the requested tools and loop again while it is `"tool_use"`, and finish the job only when it is `"end_turn"`.
options.explanation: The API reports why each response ended, so the loop should read that instead of the text: `"tool_use"` means Claude wants tools run and results returned, `"end_turn"` means it has finished. A plan that quotes the phrase no longer stops the job after one file. A cap can stay as a safety net, but not as the stopping rule.

options.text: Ask Claude to send its plan in a separate first response with no tool calls, and keep the text check for the responses that follow it.
options.explanation: This tries to control the shape of each response with an instruction, which Claude follows most of the time but not always, and any later response that restates the plan still ends the job. The real cause, a loop that parses text to decide when to stop, stays in place.

questions.keyConcept: End an agentic loop on `stop_reason`, continuing on `"tool_use"` and stopping on `"end_turn"`, not on phrases in Claude's text.

questions.stem: Cobalt Pay's review coordinator spawns the security, bug and test reviewers with the `Task` tool and posts one summary per PR; under PCI, a card-handling service left unreviewed must block the merge. To cover the 14 card-handling services, the security reviewer now spawns its own per-service subagents, and its prompt tells it to name any service it could not review. On PR #9132 the card-vault subagent timed out, the security reviewer's final message read "No issues found", and the coordinator posted "no security findings". What should change?

options.text: Have the coordinator spawn the 14 per-service security reviewers itself, and treat a reviewer that times out as having no findings, so one slow service does not hold up the merge.
